title: Installation
text: What you need, and how to make a site for a tool. toolsite is a template. You copy it once per tool, and each copy becomes that tool's site.

title: What you need
text: - Node 22 or later. - The GitHub CLI, logged in, if you want to publish to GitHub Pages.

title: Get the template
text: git clone https://github.com/rynf1t/toolsite Keep it somewhere you'll find it again, like ~/Projects/toolsite . You never edit the template to make a site. You make a copy.

title: Make a site
text: toolsite/scripts/new-site.sh mytool This makes mytool-site next to the template, with a starter config, one docs page, a fresh git repository and its packages installed. Add --from with your tool's folder and it also brings across the tool's docs/ folder, or its README if there's no docs/ : toolsite/scripts/new-site.sh mytool --from ~/Projects/mytool To publish on your own domain, add --domain . The site goes to mytool.example.com , and the deploy adds the DNS record if the domain is on Cloudflare: toolsite/scripts/new-site.sh mytool --from ~/Projects/mytool --domain example.com The quick start goes from here to a published site.

title: Quick start
text: From an empty site to a published one. Four steps: make the site, fill in the config, write the docs, publish.

title: 1. Make the site
text: toolsite/scripts/new-site.sh mytool --from ~/Projects/mytool cd mytool-site npm run dev The dev server prints an address, usually http://localhost:5173 . Keep it open while you work. It reloads on every save.

title: 2. Fill in the config
text: Open site.config.ts . Every TODO: needs a real value: the one sentence that says what the tool is, the install command and what it needs to run. The two colour hues start out picked from the name. Change them if you like. Configuration covers every field.

title: 3. Write the docs
text: Each page is a Markdown file in content/docs , named like 03-commands.md . The number sets the order. Writing docs has the conventions.

title: 4. Publish
text: scripts/deploy-pages.sh The first run creates a public GitHub repository for the site and turns on Pages. After that, the same command updates it. GitHub usually has it live within a minute. See Deploying for your own domain.

title: Configuration
text: Every field in site.config.ts. site.config.ts holds everything that makes the site about your tool. The landing page, its Markdown copy, llms.txt , the header, the favicon and the colours all read from it.

title: Fields
text: Field What it's for name The tool's name, as you'd write it in a sentence. Shown in the header and page titles. description One sentence a stranger understands. Used in meta tags and llms.txt . repo The tool's source. The header's GitHub link goes here. origin Where the site lives, such as https://you.github.io/mytool-site . Links in the Markdown copies are built from it. install The first command someone runs. Shown with a copy button. requirement What it needs, printed under the install line. status Optional. A short chip above the headline, such as Early or v1.2 . colours Two hues. See Colours. mark Optional. The inside of a 20 by 20 SVG for the header and favicon. hero The headline, the lead paragraph, and a screenshot or code sample. sections The landing page bands. See Sections. questions The questions at the bottom of the landing page. nav Optional. Extra header links after Docs, such as a second tool's docs group. author Optional. Who made it, as { label, href } , linked at the end of the footer. Text fields take inline Markdown: code , bold, and links. A link that starts with / is a path on this site.

title: Colours
text: colours: { tint: 255, accent: 75 }, Both are hues on the oklch colour wheel, from 0 to 360. Roughly: 25 red, 75 amber, 150 green, 200 teal, 255 blue, 300 violet. - tint nudges every grey on the page toward a hue. The greys stay grey. They just feel warm or cool. - accent is the one colour with jobs: the text caret, selection, search highlights, the status dot and one syntax colour. It appears nowhere else. Focus rings get their own hue, picked to stay clear of the accent. Light and dark palettes, shadows, the browser's theme colour and the favicon all follow from these two numbers.

title: Sections
text: Each section is a band on the landing page: copy on the left, and something to look at on the right. { eyebrow: 'Jump', title: 'Enter takes you there.', body: 'Two or three sentences. Inline code and links work.', link: { label: 'Commands', href: '/docs/commands' }, // then at most one of these items: [{ name: 'enter', text: 'Jump to the pane' }], code: ' a comment\nmytool run --json', image: { src: '/jump.webp', alt: 'The pane after a jump', width: 1600, height: 1000 } } Leave all three out and the copy stands alone. Images go in static/ . Give them width and height , the image's real pixel size, so the page doesn't jump while they load. WebP keeps them small: cwebp -q 82 shot.png -o shot.webp .

title: The hero
text: Show the tool working. Use image for a screenshot in static/ , or code for a short terminal session. In a terminal sample the first word of each command is coloured as the program, and lines starting with are comments. For a live demo, add src/custom/Hero.svelte . See Custom hero and styles.

title: Writing docs
text: File names, front matter and the conventions every page follows. Each docs page is one Markdown file in content/docs . The site builds the page, the sidebar, search, the Markdown copy and the llms.txt entry from it.

title: File names
text: Name files with a number and a slug, like 03-commands.md . The number sets the order and the slug becomes the address, so this one lives at /docs/commands . The first page is where /docs opens, and it should be Installation.

title: Front matter
text: title: Commands description: Every command, its flags and what it prints. group: Reference group makes the sidebar headings. Pages with the same group sit together, in file order.

title: The lead
text: Make the first paragraph bold, and only that, and it becomes the page's lead: larger, and in full ink. Use it for the one or two sentences that answer what this page is for.

title: Headings
text: Use for sections. Each one gets a link on hover, an entry under the page in the sidebar, and its own result in search. Keep them short and say what's in them.

title: Code
text: Fenced code blocks get syntax colours and a copy button. Name the language after the fence. The ones built in are sh , go , json , lua , ts , js , yaml , toml , swift , python and rust . Add more in src/lib/docs.server.ts .

title: Links
text: Link to other pages by path, like Commands . The site adds the base path when it's published under a subfolder, and the Markdown copies turn these links into full addresses that point at other Markdown copies.

title: Good docs pages
text: - Open at installation. Someone arriving cold should get to a working command in one page. - Put limits next to the feature they limit. - Write errors and fixes together: what you'll see, and what to do. - Prefer prose to bullet lists, and tables for anything with two or more fields.

title: Changelog
text: Dated release notes, one Markdown file each. Release notes live in content/changelog , one file per release. Once there's one, the header gets a Changelog link.

title: File names
text: Name each file with its date and a slug, like 2026-11-10-toasts.md . The date sets the order, newest first, and the whole name becomes the address: /changelog/2026-11-10-toasts .

title: Front matter
text: title: Toasts when an agent needs you description: One line for llms.txt and search. version: 0.3.0 version is optional. It shows under the title.

title: Writing an entry
text: Make the first paragraph bold. It becomes the lead on the changelog page, so it should say what changed for the reader in a sentence or two. Then one section per change. Say what's different now, and what it replaces if anything.

title: What the site makes from it
text: - /changelog : every entry, newest first, with its lead and a link to the full post. - /changelog/SLUG : the full post. - /changelog.md and /changelog/SLUG.md : Markdown copies for agents. - llms.txt lists the ten newest. llms-full.txt and search include every entry.

title: Custom hero and styles
text: A live demo on the landing page, and site-specific CSS. A site can bring its own code in src/custom . Template updates never touch that folder.

title: A custom hero
text: Add src/custom/Hero.svelte and the landing page shows it in place of the hero screenshot or code sample. It gets the right-hand column, about 30rem wide on a desktop and the full width on a phone. Keep it light: it runs on every visit to the home page. Anything the hero imports, like data for a demo, goes in src/custom too.

title: Custom styles
text: Every .css file in src/custom loads on every page, after the template's styles. Use the colour tokens from src/app.css , like --ink , --soft , --accent and --surface , so both light and dark work. Colours that only make sense for this tool can go there as new tokens. Define the dark version under :root[data-mode='dark'] .

title: Everything else
text: Changes anywhere else in src are the template's, and scripts/update-site.sh replaces them. If a site needs something the template can't do, add it to the template so every site gets it.

title: Deploying
text: Publishing to GitHub Pages, and using your own domain. scripts/deploy-pages.sh builds the site and publishes it to GitHub Pages. Run it again whenever you change something.

title: What it does
text: 1. Stops if site.config.ts still has a TODO: in it. 2. Creates a public GitHub repository for the site, named after its folder, if there isn't one. 3. Pushes main . 4. Builds the site for the address in origin . 5. Replaces the gh-pages branch with the build and turns on Pages. Pages needs a public repository on a free GitHub plan. The site's repository is separate from your tool's, so the tool can stay private.

title: Your own domain
text: Set origin in site.config.ts to the address, like https://mytool.example.com , and deploy. The script sees the domain isn't on github.io, so it builds without a subfolder, adds the CNAME file and tells GitHub about the domain. If the domain's DNS is on Cloudflare, the script adds the DNS record too. It needs a Cloudflare token for that, which you save once per Mac: scripts/cloudflare-token.sh It opens Cloudflare's token page, checks the token you paste, and keeps it in your login keychain. From then on every deploy makes sure there's a DNS-only CNAME from the domain to your github.io address. It never replaces a record that points somewhere else. It tells you what's there and stops. Without a token, add that CNAME yourself. Leave Cloudflare's proxy off for it, so GitHub can issue the certificate. HTTPS usually works within a few minutes, and the next deploy switches on HTTPS only.

title: Taking a site down
text: scripts/remove-site.sh --yes It stops GitHub Pages serving the site, deletes its Cloudflare DNS record if it points at GitHub, and archives the repository. The archive keeps everything, read-only, so you can bring it back later.

title: Somewhere else
text: npm run build writes a plain static site to build/ . Any static host can serve it. Set VITE_ORIGIN to the address, and VITE_BASE too if it lives under a subfolder.

title: Updating a site
text: Pulling template improvements into an existing site. Each site is a copy of the template, so it doesn't change on its own. scripts/update-site.sh brings it up to date.

title: Run it
text: scripts/update-site.sh npm run check && npm run build git diff Commit when you're happy with it. The script won't run with uncommitted changes, so the update is always a diff of its own.

title: What it changes
text: The template's code: src (apart from src/custom ), the scripts, AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md and the build config. It takes the template's package.json but keeps your site's name, and runs npm install if the packages changed. It records the template version in .toolsite-version .

title: What it leaves alone
text: site.config.ts , content , static , src/custom and README.md . Those are the site's.

title: Where the template comes from
text: --template DIR if you give it, then $TOOLSITE_TEMPLATE , then ~/Projects/toolsite , and otherwise a fresh clone from GitHub.

title: Agents
text: How a coding agent builds a site, and how agents read one. Agents are first-class readers and writers here. They can make a site for you, and every published page is there for them as Markdown.

title: Having an agent build the site
text: Each site carries an AGENTS.md with the rules: where things go, what each config field is for, and what good copy looks like. To have an agent build a site, ask it something like: Make a toolsite for ~/Projects/mytool. Run new-site.sh with --from, then fill in site.config.ts and content/docs from the tool's code and README. Show me the dev server before deploying.

title: Reading a published site
text: - Add .md to any docs address for the page as Markdown, with front matter. - /index.md is the landing page as Markdown. - /llms.txt lists every page with its description. /llms-full.txt is every page in one file. - /search.json is the search index, one entry per section. Links inside the Markdown copies point at other Markdown copies, so an agent can follow them without parsing HTML.

title: Limits
text: What toolsite doesn't do, and how to work around it. One landing page and one docs set per site. A few things are out of scope on purpose.

title: Two tools on one site
text: A site has one landing page. If two tools ship together, give the second its own sidebar group with group: craftkit in its pages' front matter, and add a header link with nav in site.config.ts . If it stands on its own, give it its own site.

title: DNS only on Cloudflare
text: The deploy script can add DNS records on Cloudflare. Anywhere else, add the CNAME yourself once per domain.

title: GitHub Pages needs a public repository
text: On a free GitHub plan, so the site's source is public. The tool's own repository can stay private, because the site lives in a separate one.

title: Template code is the template's
text: scripts/update-site.sh replaces everything in src outside src/custom . Put site-specific code in src/custom , or add the feature to the template.

title: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
page: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
text: Four things the first version couldn't do. Sites can now keep release notes, readers can pick light or dark, a site can bring its own hero demo, and existing sites can pull in template improvements.

title: Changelog
page: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
text: Put dated Markdown files in content/changelog , named like 2026-11-10-what-changed.md . The site adds a Changelog link to the header, an index page, a page per entry, Markdown copies and entries in llms.txt . See Changelog.

title: Light and dark
page: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
text: There's now a switch in the header and the docs sidebar. Pages still follow the system until a reader picks, and the choice is remembered.

title: Custom heroes
page: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
text: Drop a Hero.svelte into src/custom and it replaces the sample on the landing page. CSS files there load on every page. Template updates never touch that folder.

title: Template updates
page: Changelog, a light and dark switch, custom heroes and template updates
text: scripts/update-site.sh brings a site up to the latest template. It replaces the template's code and leaves your words, images and src/custom alone. See Updating a site.

title: Faster pages, smoother moves, and taking a site down
page: Faster pages, smoother moves, and taking a site down
text: Search that's ready before you open it, page cross-fades, and remove-site.sh. Pages load and move faster, and a site can now be taken down with one command.

title: Faster and smoother
page: Faster pages, smoother moves, and taking a site down
text: - Search fetches its index as soon as you hover or focus the search button, so results are there the moment it opens. - Pages cross-fade in 150ms. The header and the docs sidebar stay still while the page changes. With Reduce Motion on, pages switch instantly. - The text font is preloaded, so headings don't reflow as it arrives. - Images take a width and height , so the page doesn't jump while they load. The hero here is now a 56 KB WebP.

title: Taking a site down
page: Faster pages, smoother moves, and taking a site down
text: scripts/remove-site.sh --yes stops GitHub Pages serving the site, deletes its DNS record on Cloudflare, and archives the repository. See Deploying.
